transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I’ve taken on way too much lately—new projects, workshops, fixing up the studio, client calls. It all seemed manageable at first, but now the deadlines are piling up, and I’m worried about the mortgage.
How long have you been feeling this overwhelmed and worried about your workload and finances—days, weeks, or longer?
About three months, I think—since I took on the mortgage for the cottage-studio.

Over these past three months, have you noticed needing much less sleep than usual while still feeling full of energy, or taking on new projects because you felt unusually confident or 'on top of the world'?

I did take on more because I felt unusually sure of myself. I started believing my illustrations could become the visual language scientific journals had been missing for decades, and that I was the one person who could really make that happen.
Before these past three months, have you ever had a period—lasting two weeks or more—where you felt persistently sad, low on energy, or lost interest in things you used to enjoy?
I’m not sure. I can’t really think of a stretch like that before this.
Before these last three months, have you ever had another period—separate from this one—where you felt unusually elevated, energetic, or overly confident for several days or more?
I don’t think so. Nothing else like this comes to mind before the past few months.

When you think about your illustrations transforming scientific journals, do you feel this is an absolute certainty that nothing could convince you otherwise, or do you see it more as a strong hope or ambition?

It felt like certainty. I know it sounds extreme, but I became convinced that a couple of clients, and even an editor, were trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled the system. They reassured me, but it really didn’t settle me.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a distinct ~3-month period characterized by elevated, unusually confident mood, decreased need for sleep with increased energy, excessive involvement in multiple goal-directed activities (new projects, workshops, studio renovation), and grandiosity that reached delusional intensity (belief that his illustrations were the definitive missing 'visual language' for scientific journals, and that others were trying to steal his work before he could reveal it). These grandiose and persecutory beliefs were fixed and not modifiable by reassurance, indicating psychotic features accompanying the manic episode. There is no history of a prior depressive episode, making this a single manic episode with psychotic symptoms rather than bipolar disorder (which requires a prior mood episode of opposite polarity) or schizophrenia-spectrum illness (where mood symptoms would not be the primary organizing feature and psychosis would predate or exist independent of mood disturbance).

confirmed_symptoms: Decreased need for sleep with high energy
Increased goal-directed activity (multiple new projects, workshops, studio renovation)
Grandiosity regarding professional abilities and impact
Fixed grandiose belief that his illustrations were uniquely destined to transform scientific journals
Persecutory/paranoid belief that clients and an editor were trying to steal his work
Belief maintained despite reassurance, consistent with delusional conviction

additional_requirements: No prior depressive episode identified, ruling out bipolar disorder classification
No prior manic or hypomanic episode identified, confirming this as a single episode
Delusional content (grandiose/persecutory) confirmed as mood-congruent and temporally linked to the manic episode, supporting psychotic features rather than a primary psychotic disorder
